instructions: Peel the potatoes and cut them into 1/2-inch cubes. Chop the onion and the bell pepper into small pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a 10-inch nonstick skillet over medium heat. Add the potatoes and 1/2 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes, stirring now and then, until the edges are golden.
Add the onion and the bell pepper and cook for 6 minutes, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are tender when you poke one with a fork.
While they cook, grate the Parmesan until you have 1/3 cup. Whisk the eggs in a large bowl with the Parmesan and 1/2 tsp salt.

Pour the eggs over the vegetables. Stir gently for about 1 minute, until the edges start to set, then stop stirring. Turn the heat to medium-low and cook for 5 minutes, until the bottom is browned and the top is almost set.

Slide the frittata onto a large plate. Put the pan upside down over the plate, hold them together with oven mitts and flip. Cook the second side for 3 minutes, until it's golden and set all the way through.
Slide the frittata onto a cutting board and let it cool for 5 minutes. Cut it into 8 wedges.
Halve the garlic clove and cut the tomato in half. Rub one side of each of the 8 bread slices with the cut garlic, then with a cut tomato, and sprinkle each with a pinch of salt.
Set 2 wedges on each of 4 slices, tomato side up, and close the sandwiches. Brush the outside of the bread with the last 1 tbsp of oil.

Wipe out the skillet and heat it over medium heat. Press 2 sandwiches at a time under a heavy pan or a panini press for 3 minutes, flip, and press the other side for 3 minutes, until the bread is golden and crisp.
Cut each sandwich in half and serve warm.
To make the frittata ahead, cook it through step 7, wrap the wedges and refrigerate them for up to 3 days. Build and press the sandwiches when you're ready to eat.
method_notes: None of the three versions has a rating, so this is a fallback lead. Mary Ann Esposito's frittata sandwich is the meatless one the list describes: a potato, onion and pepper frittata, with the bread rubbed with garlic and tomato. The Chicago Tribune frittata panini supplies the pressed, toasted finish, though its caramelized onions and sausage are left out. Eggland's Best bakes a frittata in a sheet pan and cuts it in squares, which is the make-ahead idea. This version uses 8 eggs, not 10, to fit a 10-inch pan and four sandwiches.
